title: Todoist vs Notion in 2026: Which To-Do App Wins?
body_md:
![todoist.com official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/todoist-vs-notion-in-2026-which-to-do-app-wins/1.png)
*Screenshot of todoist.com ([source](https://www.todoist.com/pricing))*

**Short answer:** If you want a fast, reliable place to capture and finish tasks, pick Todoist. If your tasks are tangled up with notes, docs, project trackers, and a team wiki, pick Notion. Todoist is the better *to-do app*; Notion is the better *workspace that can hold a to-do list* — and the price gap between them is wider than most people expect.

## Quick Comparison

![todoist.com official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/todoist-vs-notion-in-2026-which-to-do-app-wins/2.png)
*Screenshot of todoist.com ([source](https://www.todoist.com/help/articles/todoist-plans-pricing-and-billing-faq-Vq2z0HWL6))*

| Comparison | **Todoist** | **Notion** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Free plan** | Beginner: free forever, 5 personal projects, Smart Quick Add, list & board layouts, 3 filters | Free: unlimited pages/blocks for a solo user, 10 guests, 5 MB file uploads, 7-day page history |
| **Entry paid plan** | Pro — $5/user/mo billed yearly ($60/yr), $7/mo month-to-month | Plus — $10/member/mo billed yearly, $12/mo month-to-month |
| **Team plan** | Business — $8/user/mo yearly ($96/user/yr), $10/user/mo monthly | Business — $20/member/mo billed yearly, $24/mo monthly |
| **Top tier** | None — Business is the ceiling | Enterprise — custom quote |
| **Core strength** | Fast task capture, natural-language dates, recurring tasks, filters | Databases, docs, wikis, custom views, all-in-one workspace |
| **Built-in AI** | AI features on paid plans (Task Assist, Ramble) | Full Notion AI requires the Business tier |
| **Learning curve** | Low — usable in ten minutes | Medium to high — you build your own system |
| **Best for** | Individuals and small teams who want tasks done | Teams that want tasks, docs, and knowledge in one place |

Prices are US dollars, before tax, as listed by each vendor; both companies bill per user/member and discount annual billing.

## Pricing: Todoist Is Roughly Half the Cost

![notion.com official page screenshot](https://afroditena.github.io/mattress-checklist-android/assets/img/todoist-vs-notion-in-2026-which-to-do-app-wins/3.png)
*Screenshot of notion.com ([source](https://www.notion.com/pricing))*

Todoist keeps it simple. It offers three plans: Beginner (free), Pro, and Business.

Pro runs $5/month billed annually ($60/year) or $7/month billed monthly, and Business is $8/user/month annually ($96/user/year) or $10/user/month monthly. Worth knowing: prices went up in December 2025 — Pro rose from $4 to $5 and Business from $6 to $8 on annual billing, so older articles quoting $4 are out of date. Long-time subscribers may sit on a "Pro Legacy" plan that preserves an older rate; that was Todoist's stated policy at the time of writing, and newer paid features aren't necessarily added to it.

Notion has four tiers — Free, Plus, Business, and Enterprise — and costs more per seat. Plus is $12 per member monthly or $10 billed yearly, and Business is $24 monthly or $20 per member per month billed yearly. Notion's pricing page defaults to the "Pay yearly" toggle and labels those annual rates "per member / month," which is exactly how people end up budgeting the wrong number. There's also a metered layer on top: agent usage is billed separately in credits.

Run the math for a five-person team on annual billing and Todoist Business lands around $480/year versus roughly $600/year for Notion Plus — and $1,200/year if that team needs Notion Business. That doesn't make Notion overpriced; it's doing far more than task tracking. But if tasks are all you need, you're paying a premium for capability you won't use.

## Ease of Use: Opinionated vs. Open-Ended

Todoist is opinionated, and that's the point. You type "email Dana about the Q3 deck Friday 9am p1," and it parses the date, time, and priority for you. Smart Quick Add, task reminders, and list and board layouts are available on the free Beginner plan. There's essentially no setup phase — you install it and start dumping tasks.

Notion is the opposite: a blank canvas. You manage tasks through Kanban boards, calendar and list views, track related information on each item, change statuses, collaborate, and work with spreadsheet-style databases. That flexibility is genuinely powerful, but you're the architect.

A Notion task system is something you *design* — properties, filtered views, relations between a tasks database and a projects database — and then maintain. Some people love that. Others spend a weekend building a gorgeous dashboard and never open it again.

A useful gut check: if you've ever abandoned a productivity system because tweaking it became the hobby, Todoist's guardrails are a feature, not a limitation.

## The Feature That Actually Separates Them

Todoist's edge is *capture speed and nudging*. Recurring tasks, natural-language scheduling, priority flags, and saved filters are the everyday machinery of getting things done, and Todoist has spent years polishing them. Pro adds the calendar layout, task durations and 300 projects — the upgrade that turns a list into a day plan.

Notion's edge is *context*. A task in Notion isn't just a line of text — it's a page that can hold the meeting notes, the spec, the client brief, and a link to the parent project. For knowledge work where "the task" and "the document" are inseparable, that's a real advantage no standalone to-do app can match.

The trade-off shows up in daily friction. Adding a quick task in Notion takes more clicks and more thought about where it belongs, and mobile capture has never been as instant as Todoist's. Conversely, Todoist can't hold your team wiki, and it won't replace a project database with rollups and relations.

## Collaboration and AI

For teams, Todoist's Business plan is deliberately narrow: a shared team workspace, up to 500 team projects, calendar layout for team projects, granular activity logs, shared templates, 1,000 team members and guests, team project folders, roles and permissions, and centralized billing, plus SOC 2 Type II certification listed on the pricing page, which matters if procurement has to sign off. That's a solid shared task layer — not a full project management suite. No Gantt charts, no dependencies.

Notion scales differently. Page history stretches from 7 days on Free to 30 on Plus, 90 on Business, and unlimited on Enterprise, with Enterprise adding provisioning, audit logs, and a dedicated customer success manager. Business also raises the API limit from 180 to 600 requests a minute per connection, which is the kind of detail only integration-heavy teams notice — until a nightly sync crawls.

AI is where budgets diverge most. Full Notion AI stopped being a $10 add-on in May 2025 and now lives on Business, so if you want Notion and AI, the floor is $20, not $10. Business includes Notion Agent, AI Meeting Notes and Enterprise Search, while Free and Plus only get a limited trial.

Todoist's AI sits on its far cheaper paid plans, but it's narrower in scope — it helps you phrase, break down, and organize tasks rather than summarize documents or search a knowledge base.

## Who Should Use Which

- **Solo professionals and freelancers tracking personal work:** Todoist. Pro at $60/year is hard to beat, and the free tier is genuinely usable if you stay under five projects.
- **Students and casual list-makers:** Todoist Beginner, free. Notion's free tier also works well if you want notes and tasks together, and eligible students and teachers can get a one-member Plus workspace free.
- **Small teams sharing a task list:** Todoist Business. It's well under half the per-seat cost of Notion Business and requires no system-building.
- **Teams whose work lives in docs, wikis, and trackers:** Notion. Tasks-plus-context in one workspace is worth the extra spend, and it consolidates tools you're probably paying for separately.
- **Teams that want built-in AI over their own content:** Notion Business — just budget the $20/seat honestly, plus credits if you lean on agents.
- **People who've bounced off complex tools before:** Todoist, every time.
- **Honestly? Many people run both:** Notion as the knowledge base, Todoist as the daily action list. The combined cost is still modest, and each tool does what it's actually good at.

## FAQ

**Can Notion fully replace Todoist?**
Functionally, yes — you can build a task database with due dates, priorities, and recurring items. Practically, it depends on whether you'll accept slower capture and weaker reminders in exchange for keeping everything in one place.

**Is Todoist's free plan enough?**
For a lot of people, yes. Beginner is $0 with 5 personal projects, list and board layouts, task reminders, 3 custom filters and one week of activity history. The project cap is the usual reason to upgrade.

**Which is cheaper for a 10-person team?**
Todoist, clearly. Business runs $96 per user per year on annual billing, which is $960. For a ten-person team, Notion is $1,200 a year on Plus and $2,400 on Business.

**Do I have to pay annually to get the advertised price?**
Effectively, yes. Every headline Todoist price is the annual rate, and monthly billing costs roughly 40% more — $7 vs. $5 on Pro, $10 vs. $8 on Business. Notion works the same way, so confirm the toggle on each vendor's pricing page before you commit a budget line — both companies have changed prices recently.

## My Take

I think most people shopping for a "to-do app" and seriously considering Notion are solving the wrong problem. If you catch yourself designing a tasks database before you've written down the tasks, that's the tell. Buy Todoist Pro, use it for a month, and see whether the thing you were missing was ever the software.

My read on the pricing is that the AI repackaging is the real story here. Moving full Notion AI to Business doubled the entry cost for anyone who wants it, from $10 to $20 per member a month. That's a defensible business decision, but it means "Notion is only $10" is now a misleading sentence for most teams evaluating it in 2026.

The fair point for Notion's side: for teams whose actual output is documents, a task manager that can't hold the document is a permanent tax. Clicking between two apps forty times a day is its own kind of expensive, and the per-seat gap can disappear if Notion lets you cancel a wiki tool and a docs tool.

What I'd watch is Todoist's price trajectory. A 25–33% annual-plan increase in December 2025 is not nothing, and a product with no tier above Business has one obvious lever left. I'd still pay $60 a year for it, but I'd stop treating that number as fixed.

I'm not a financial or procurement professional, so treat the seat math here as arithmetic to check against your own vendor quotes, not advice on how to spend your company's money.
